# Client-Side Prediction and Reconciliation

Under [[server-authoritative-netcode]] the client owns no state — but waiting a round trip before the
player's own avatar moves is unplayable. Prediction resolves this: the client runs the same movement
simulation locally and immediately, then corrects itself when the authoritative snapshot arrives.

Two halves, and they are usually confused:

- **Prediction** — apply the local input to the local avatar now, using a copy of the server's
  movement code.
- **Reconciliation** — when a snapshot arrives showing a different position, get back to the
  server's answer without the correction looking like a teleport.

## The two reconciliation strategies

**Input replay (the textbook form).** Keep every unacknowledged input in a buffer. On correction,
snap to the server position, then re-simulate every buffered input on top of it. This is *correct* —
the client converges to exactly what the server will compute — at the cost of a buffer, sequence
numbers on both sides, and a simulation that must be replayable from an arbitrary state.

**Blend toward snapshot (what [[stickfps]] ships).** No replay, no buffer. `reconcile()` snaps
outright when the error exceeds 3 m, and otherwise closes 15% of the gap per call. Errors decay
geometrically instead of being cancelled.

The repo names the limit itself rather than implying the stronger property:

> "Full input-replay reconciliation (re-simulating unacknowledged inputs after a server correction)
> is not implemented — v1 uses a simpler blend-toward-snapshot approach... Fine at low latency, will
> feel soft under real internet jitter."
> — browser_game_stickfps/PROGRESS.md, 2026-07-25

**Do not read this page as documenting input replay.** The percentage blend is the whole mechanism.
Its failure mode is exactly the one quoted: under jitter the local avatar is persistently a little
behind its own inputs and the controls feel rubbery, because a correction is never fully paid off
before the next one lands.

## Why the blend is defensible here

Prediction only needs to cover *movement*, because shooting is a request, not a claim — the client
never predicts a hit, so a mispredicted position can never produce a wrong kill. The worst outcome of
a soft correction is a few centimetres of visual drift. That is the design property that makes the
cheap strategy affordable, and it is the thing to check before copying it: **prediction can be
approximate only where nothing scored depends on it.**

Prediction also requires the client to hold a duplicate of the server's movement code, kept in sync
by hand — see [[duplicate-sim-code-over-shared-package]]. Both copies step at the same rate under
[[fixed-timestep-simulation]]; if the rates diverge, prediction error grows with no bound and the
blend never catches up.

## Not the same as interpolating others

Prediction is for the local player, who is ahead of the server. [[entity-interpolation]] is for
remote players, who are deliberately rendered behind it. A build can have one and not the other, and
they fail in visibly different ways.
